name: Ulagalantha Perumal Temple, Tirukoilur
deity: Vishnu as Ulagalantha Perumal (Trivikrama), the Lord who measured the worlds, with the Goddess Poongothai (Pushpavalli)
period: A Divya Desam of Nadu Nadu on the Pennai, sung by the Mudhal Alvars and Thirumangai Alvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham
dynasty: Medieval Chola, with Vijayanagara and Madurai Nayak additions
summary: At Tirukoilur on the Pennai, Vishnu stands as Trivikrama, the Lord who measured the worlds — the Divya Desam where tradition says the first three Alvars met on a night of rain and the Prabandham began.

sections.history: Tirukoilur, on the Thenpennai river, is one of the 108 Divya Desams and among the most revered shrines of Nadu Nadu. Its place in Sri Vaishnava memory is unique: tradition holds that here the Lord revealed himself to Poigai, Bhoothath and Pey Alvar — the Mudhal Alvars, the first three of the twelve — and that here they sang the three Thiruvandhadhis that open the Nalayira Divya Prabandham. Thirumangai Alvar later praised the same Lord. The temple as it stands is believed to have been built by the Medieval Cholas, and the Vijayanagara kings and the Madurai Nayaks added to it in later centuries. Worship has continued through all these eras, and the town remains a centre of pilgrimage.
sections.architecture: The temple is announced from afar by its rajagopuram, which rises about 59 metres (192 feet) and is counted among the tallest temple towers in Tamil Nadu — by Wikipedia's reckoning the third tallest. Beyond it lie the enclosures and pillared halls of the Dravidian plan, with the sanctum of Trivikrama at the centre and the Goddess Poongothai in her own shrine. The presiding image shows the Lord in his giant striding form, one foot lifted to measure the heavens.
sections.legends: Two stories meet here. The first is that of Vamana: Vishnu came as a dwarf to King Mahabali, asked for three paces of land, and grew into Trivikrama, measuring earth and sky in two strides. The second belongs to the Alvars. On a night of storm, the sthala tradition tells, Poigai Alvar sheltered in a narrow passage, and Bhoothath and Pey Alvar came in after him, until the three stood pressed together — and felt a fourth among them. Poigai lit a lamp of verse with the earth as its bowl and the sea as its oil, Bhoothath with love as the lamp, and Pey Alvar beheld the Lord.
sections.festivals: The Brahmotsavam in Panguni (March–April) is the temple's principal festival, with the processional deity carried through the town on its vahanas. An Andal utsavam is also kept, and Vaikunta Ekadashi and the Alvars' birth-stars are observed with particular devotion in this, the Alvars' own meeting place.
sections.experience: Approach on foot to feel the great tower grow overhead, then stand before Trivikrama and recall the three Alvars who, tradition says, met here in the dark and found the Lord among them. Reciting a verse of the Mudhal Thiruvandhadhi here is a quiet devotion many pilgrims keep. The Pennai and the old town around the temple reward an unhurried walk.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions and a midday closure; the Panguni Brahmotsavam and Vaikunta Ekadashi are busiest. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Tirukoilur has a railway station on the Villupuram–Katpadi line and is linked by road to Villupuram and Tiruvannamalai; Chennai has the nearest major airport, a few hours away by road.
